name: EC Sportz
tagline: Management software for sports academies: students, batches, coaches, attendance and fee collection in one portal.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Underneath the branding this is a roster plus a calendar plus a fee ledger, and an agent can scaffold that in a sitting. The hard part is everything that touches the outside world: online fee payments, receipts that satisfy an accountant, SMS or WhatsApp reminders parents actually read, and a phone-friendly view coaches will use on a dusty field. A single academy running one or two sports can genuinely live on a self-hosted build. The moment you have multiple branches, part-time coaches with different permissions, and parents who expect a payment link, you are rebuilding a product rather than a tool.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted web app where an admin manages students, batches and coaches, marks attendance per session, and tracks fees due and paid with simple reports.
requirements: A small server or Raspberry Pi on the academy network, or a cheap VPS
A domain plus HTTPS if parents or coaches will log in from outside
A payment gateway account if you want online fee collection instead of manual entry
Someone willing to own backups of the SQLite file
whatYouLose: Integrated online fee payment, auto receipts and dunning reminders
Parent-facing mobile app and push notifications
Role permissions and audit trails that survive staff turnover
Multi-branch and multi-sport reporting without custom work
Someone to call when fees go missing the week before a tournament
moatNotes: Once a season of attendance and fee history lives inside a system, nobody migrates mid-term. That is the real lock-in, not the feature list.
whyPeopleStillPay: Academy admins are not sysadmins. Paying for this buys payment plumbing, a parent app, and the ability to blame a vendor when a receipt is wrong, which is worth more than the software itself to a business run out of a clubhouse office. The DIY version wins only when one person is technical, motivated, and intends to stay.
notes: Vertical SaaS for a niche is usually a CRUD app with domain opinions baked in, and those opinions are most of what you are buying.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted sports academy management app for a single academy. No cloud accounts, no telemetry, no external analytics.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, schema created by a migration script on first run
- Tailwind CSS, no component library
- Single shared password login read from ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env, plus a separate COACH_PASSWORD with read-plus-attendance-only access. Sessions via a signed HTTP-only cookie.

Data model:
- students: name, date of birth, guardian name, guardian phone, sport, joined date, active flag, notes
- coaches: name, phone, sports
- batches: name, sport, coach id, days of week, start time, duration minutes, monthly fee
- enrollments: student id, batch id, start date, end date nullable
- sessions: batch id, date, status (held, cancelled)
- attendance: session id, student id, state (present, absent, late)
- payments: student id, period (YYYY-MM), amount, method, paid on, reference

Screens:
- Dashboard: active student count, today's sessions, fees outstanding this month
- Students: list with search and sport filter, detail page with enrollments, attendance rate, payment history
- Batches: list, detail with roster, generate sessions for a date range from the batch schedule
- Attendance: pick a session, mark the whole roster on one mobile-friendly screen with large tap targets, save in one request
- Fees: per month view of expected versus received per student, record a payment, mark as waived
- Reports: attendance percentage per batch per month, fee collection total per month, both exportable as CSV

In scope: all of the above, seed script with two batches and fifteen fake students, printable roster view.
Out of scope: online payment gateways, SMS or WhatsApp sending, parent logins, multi-branch, mobile apps, email.

Include a README with setup, .env.example, a one-command backup script that copies the SQLite file with a timestamp, and a restore note.
